item.title: Awaji Hanasajiki: Hillside Flower Fields Above the Sea — Guide
item.description: Hanasajiki — the name means ‘flower balcony’ — is a hillside park on the northern tip of Awaji Island, planted with vast single-colour blocks of flowers that change through the year: rape blossom and poppies in spring, salvia and marigolds in summer, and a famous sweep of cosmos in autumn. The slope faces north-east toward Osaka Bay, so the flowers are seen against sea and sky rather than a backdrop of trees, and paths run right through the plantings.

item.title: Awaji Island Onions: Japan's Sweetest — Guide
item.description: Awaji Island’s onions are a genuine local obsession. The island’s mild maritime climate, long sunshine hours and well-drained sandy soil, combined with a slow curing period hanging in open-sided sheds, produce onions with unusually high sugar and low pungency — sweet enough that Japanese cooks eat them raw in salads where other onions would be too harsh. You will see the drying sheds all over the island, roadside stands selling nets of them for a few hundred yen, and restaurants building whole menus around them: onion burgers, whole roasted onions, onion soup and, inevitably, onion ice cream.

item.title: Hyogo Nature: Mt. Rokko, Awaji Island & Coastal Trails
item.description: Hyogo Prefecture stretches across one of Japan’s most geographically diverse corridors, running from the Pacific-facing shores of the Seto Inland Sea all the way north to the dramatic cliffs and hidden beaches of the Sea of Japan coast. Between these two edges lies an interior of forested mountains, river valleys, and historic castle towns. Few Japanese prefectures can offer a visitor alpine wildflower meadows, oceanic tidal whirlpools, fishing village seascapes, and terraced rural farmland within a single day’s travel.
